URL: https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/24/global-bond-sell-off-pressures-uk-borrowing-costs-budget
The Guardian (Heather Stewart and Graeme Wearden) — published Thursday 24 September 2026 12:41 BST; LAST UPDATED Friday 25 September 2026 05:26 BST

HEADLINE: Oil price rise creates more pressure on UK policymakers before budget
STANDFIRST: Treasury sources concede 'less room' for manoeuvre as global bond selloff also hikes government's borrowing costs

FACTS:
- Oil prices lurched upwards again on Thursday, creating a growing headache for UK policymakers ahead of John Healey's budget next month.
- Treasury sources concede the sharp jump in oil and gas prices means they have "less room" than a month ago.
- Officials are working "at pace" on a range of possible options for supporting consumers, particularly if high prices persist, feeding through into a sharp rise in the quarterly energy price cap in January.
- Any package is expected to fall far short of the across-the-board subsidies announced by Liz Truss in 2022, with the Treasury mindful of measures already taken including Andy Burnham's VAT cut on electricity bills.
- Options are believed to include shifting more green subsidies into general taxation, or targeting help at the poorest households.
- The price of a barrel of Brent crude was up almost 5% at $108 on Thursday after reports of more military clashes between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces.
- Senior UK government figures are increasingly concerned about interest rate rises, which could push up the cost of a mortgage just as Burnham has promised voters "breathing space".
- After leaving interest rates on hold at 3.75% last week, the Bank of England said it expected the ENERGY PRICE CAP TO RISE BY AS MUCH AS 24% IN THE NEW YEAR.
- The yield on 10-year UK gilts rose to 5.39% on Thursday, approaching the 19-year high set last week.
- Analysts believe recent increases in yields have wiped out MORE THAN HALF of the £24bn "headroom" against the fiscal rules that Rachel Reeves had built up at the spring statement in March.
- Healey has repeatedly promised to meet the rules with a "buffer against uncertainty" but this is widely expected to be significantly lower than £24bn. Treasury sources insist the budget will be narrowly focused.
- Yields on 10-year US treasury bonds surged to 5.17% on Thursday, the highest level since 2007.

QUOTE (Clare Lombardelli, Bank of England Deputy Governor, in a speech on Thursday to an economic conference in Warsaw, Poland): "The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response. On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity."
QUOTE (Sarah Breeden, Bank of England Deputy Governor, to a conference at Imperial College London): "The larger and longer the shock, the more likely it is that we'll see the material second-round effects that policy needs to respond [to]."

NOTE: The Guardian describes Lombardelli as "the Bank's chief economist"; the Bank of England's own speeches page lists her as Deputy Governor. Use "Bank of England deputy governor Clare Lombardelli". Her speech text is published at https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/speech/2026/september/clare-lombardelli-speech-at-the-sixth-biennial-conference-poland (dated 24 September 2026).
